chapters.title: Chapter 6: Behavioral Macroeconomics: Bubbles, Panics, and Policy at Scale

lessons.title: Animal Spirits: Keynes, Confidence, and the Business Cycle

children.text: Every economics textbook opens with a version of the same figure: a rational firm calculating the expected return on an investment, comparing it to the cost of capital, and deciding accordingly. John Maynard Keynes, writing in the shadow of the Great Depression, looked at how businesses actually decided to invest and concluded that precise calculation was rarely what was really happening. Most of the future a business is investing into simply cannot be calculated, he argued, and when calculation runs out, confidence takes over. This final chapter of the course zooms out from individuals, businesses, and organizations to where these same behavioral forces operate at the scale of an entire economy, starting with the idea that gave this scale of psychology its name.

body.text: Keynes argued that investment, the engine of the business cycle, depends less on careful mathematical expectation than on "animal spirits," a spontaneous confidence to act despite genuine, irreducible uncertainty about the future. When that confidence is high, economies expand. When it collapses, economies can contract sharply, even without any corresponding collapse in the underlying, measurable fundamentals.

children.text: Keynes's Animal Spirits: The Original Behavioral Economics

markDefs.definition: John Maynard Keynes's term, from his 1936 General Theory, for the spontaneous confidence and urge to act that drives investment decisions under genuine uncertainty, as opposed to precise mathematical expectation.

children.text: In "The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money" (1936), Keynes devoted an entire chapter to what he called
animal spirits

. His argument predates Herbert Simon's bounded rationality by nearly two decades, and Kahneman and Tversky's founding papers by almost forty years, yet reaches a remarkably similar conclusion by a different route: real decision-makers cannot actually run the calculation classical theory assumes, because the information needed simply doesn't exist yet, and confidence, convention, and a plain urge to act fill the gap calculation leaves behind.
Risk vs Uncertainty: The Knightian Distinction

markDefs.definition: Economist Frank Knight's 1921 distinction between risk, where possible outcomes and their probabilities are knowable, and uncertainty, where the future's possible outcomes and probabilities are genuinely unknowable in advance.

children.text: Keynes's argument rests on a distinction economist Frank Knight had drawn fifteen years earlier, between
risk and uncertainty

. Risk means the possible outcomes and their odds are genuinely knowable, an insurance actuarial table, a fair coin toss. Uncertainty means the future's possible outcomes aren't knowable in any meaningful, quantifiable sense at all. Most textbook decision problems, including several exercises earlier in this course, are framed as risk, because risk is what's teachable with a clean formula. Most real investment decisions, Keynes argued, are genuine Knightian uncertainty, which is precisely why animal spirits, not expected value, end up doing the real work.

body.title: The kind of problem Keynes said real business isn't
body.prompt: A factory owner considers a ₹2 crore investment with a genuinely quantifiable 60% chance of generating ₹5 crore in return, and a 40% chance of generating ₹0. What is the net expected value of this investment, in ₹ crore, after subtracting the ₹2 crore cost?
body.explanation: (0.6 × ₹5 crore) − ₹2 crore = ₹3 crore − ₹2 crore = ₹1 crore net expected value. This is a clean risk problem, exactly the kind classical economics can solve precisely. Keynes's point wasn't that this maths is wrong. It's that almost no real investment decision actually comes with these clearly known percentages attached, which is why real decisions lean so heavily on confidence instead.

Confidence, convention, and Keynes's animal spirits

children.text: Why This Matters More at the Macro Level Than the Micro Level

Chapter 3 covered how a bank can fail purely because enough depositors expect enough other depositors to withdraw, with the bank's actual fundamentals never having to change at all. Keynes's animal spirits describe the same logic at the scale of an entire economy's investment decisions. If enough businesses expect growth, they invest, hire, and produce the growth they expected. If confidence collapses, across an economy simultaneously, businesses pull back investment together, and that collective pullback can itself cause the very contraction everyone feared, regardless of what the underlying productive capacity of the economy actually was the week before. Confidence isn't merely a reaction to the business cycle in this view. It's one of the forces that produces it.
Akerlof and Shiller: Reviving Animal Spirits for Modern Macroeconomics

In 2009, Nobel laureates George Akerlof and Robert Shiller published "Animal Spirits: How Human Psychology Drives the Economy, and Why It Matters for Global Capitalism," deliberately reviving Keynes's term for the era of formal behavioral economics. They organized their argument around five psychological forces shaping macroeconomic outcomes: confidence, fairness, corruption and bad faith, money illusion, the tendency to think in nominal rather than inflation-adjusted terms, and stories, the shared narratives an economy tells itself about what's happening and what's likely to happen next. Akerlof won his Nobel in 2001 for work on markets with asymmetric information, and Shiller won his in 2013 for empirical work on asset prices, bringing this course's running thread of Nobel Prizes rooted in challenging pure rational-agent models to a genuinely macro scale.
Narrative Economics: How Stories Move Markets

markDefs.definition: Robert Shiller's argument, from his 2019 book of the same name, that popular, viral economic narratives, not only hard data, can themselves become a genuine driving force behind economic booms and contractions.

children.text: Shiller extended this argument further in his 2019 book "
Narrative Economics

": a widely repeated story, "prices only go up," "this technology changes everything," "a recession is coming," can spread through a population much like an information cascade spreads through a sequence of individual choices, except here what's spreading isn't an observed action but a shared belief. India's startup funding pullback of 2022 and 2023 carried exactly this texture: as a "funding winter" narrative took hold, many individually sound companies found capital harder to raise, not necessarily because their own fundamentals had deteriorated, but because the story investors were telling each other about the sector as a whole had changed.
Measuring Confidence: The RBI's Consumer Confidence Survey

Animal spirits sound impossible to measure, which is exactly why central banks try to measure them anyway. The RBI runs a periodic Consumer Confidence Survey, tracking households' sentiment on the general economic situation, employment, income, and spending, both current perception and future expectation. This is a direct, practical attempt to quantify Keynes's ninety-year-old concept as a usable input into policy, a thread this chapter picks back up in its final lesson on central bank behavioral policy.

body.title: Diagnosing a slowdown
body.scenario: A mid-sized manufacturing firm's order book, balance sheet, and product demand all look essentially unchanged from six months ago. Yet the CEO has quietly paused a planned factory expansion, citing "the mood out there" rather than any specific number that has moved.
body.prompt: Using Keynes's framework from this lesson, is the CEO's reasoning necessarily irrational, and what would you want to know before judging the decision?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Not necessarily irrational. If the expansion decision genuinely involves Knightian uncertainty, demand three years out, competitor behavior, financing conditions, then there was never a precise expected-value calculation underlying the original plan in the first place, only confidence that has since dropped.
2. It's worth checking whether "the mood out there" reflects a real, if hard-to-quantify, signal, other firms in the sector pulling back, credit conditions tightening, versus a purely self-referential narrative the CEO has absorbed from headlines without any grounding in the firm's own specific situation.
3. If enough other firms in the same position are also pausing simultaneously, the CEO's caution is a rational response to a genuine multiple-equilibria risk, similar to the bank-run logic from Chapter 3: pausing when others pause and expanding when others expand can each be self-fulfilling, regardless of the firm's own unchanged fundamentals.
4. The healthiest response isn't to override the caution with a spreadsheet that pretends the uncertainty isn't real, it's to ask what specific, even partial information could genuinely update the decision, rather than letting an unexamined mood alone drive it indefinitely.

body.title: Individual bias, or macro-scale animal spirits?
body.question: Which of these is the clearest example of Keynes's animal spirits operating at economy-wide scale, rather than an individual-level bias covered earlier in this course?
options: A single investor refusing to sell a losing stock out of loss aversion
A nationwide pullback in business investment after confidence falls broadly across firms, even though no specific measurable fundamental has changed
A shopper anchoring on an inflated MRP before a discount
An employee never revisiting a retirement contribution default set eight years ago
body.explanation: Option B describes confidence itself, shared and self-reinforcing across many firms simultaneously, becoming a cause of aggregate economic outcomes, which is precisely Keynes's animal spirits. The other three are individual-level biases, loss aversion, anchoring, and the default effect, operating on a single decision-maker rather than aggregating into economy-wide, self-fulfilling momentum.

body.title: Name Keynes's term
body.textWithBlank: Keynes's term for the spontaneous confidence and urge to act that drives investment under genuine, irreducible uncertainty is "___ spirits."
body.explanation: Keynes introduced animal spirits in 1936, arguing that most real investment decisions involve Knightian uncertainty rather than calculable risk, which is why confidence, not precise expected value, ends up driving them.

body.title: Did Keynes really think businesses never calculate anything?

children.text: No, and this is a common oversimplification of his argument. Keynes accepted that businesses do calculate wherever calculation is genuinely possible. His claim was narrower and, in a sense, more unsettling: for the specific, high-stakes, long-horizon decisions that drive the business cycle, whether to build a new factory, enter a new market, commit capital for a decade, the relevant future is not knowable in the way a coin flip or an actuarial table is knowable, so any precision in the underlying calculation is, in his own memorable phrase, largely a facade. The confidence behind the decision, not the spreadsheet around it, was doing most of the real work, a claim later echoed, independently, by decades of behavioral economics research this course has covered from an entirely different starting point.

body.context: Keynes's animal spirits predates Herbert Simon's 1955 bounded rationality by nearly two decades, and Kahneman and Tversky's 1974 heuristics paper by almost forty years.

points: Keynes argued that investment, the engine of the business cycle, rests less on precise calculation than on animal spirits, a spontaneous confidence to act despite genuinely unknowable future outcomes, an idea that predates the formal behavioral economics covered in Chapter 1 by decades.

Frank Knight's risk-versus-uncertainty distinction explains why: most real investment decisions face genuine uncertainty, not calculable risk, which is exactly the situation where confidence, not expected value, ends up doing the deciding.

This is the same multiple-equilibria logic Chapter 3 covered for bank runs, now applied to an entire economy's investment decisions: collective confidence or its collapse can become self-fulfilling, independent of the underlying fundamentals.

Akerlof and Shiller's 2009 revival of the concept, and Shiller's later narrative economics, extend Keynes's insight with modern tools, treating shared stories as a genuine economic force, not just noise layered on top of the real data.

The next three lessons in this final chapter build directly on this foundation: how animal spirits and information cascades combine into asset bubbles, how bank runs play out at full historical scale, and how central banks deliberately try to manage confidence as a tool of policy.
